scenario.name: AcidRain MIPS ELF Satellite Modem Wiper (/dev/mtd MEMERASE / Viasat KA-SAT)
scenario.overview: Imagine a satellite television control hub wired to tens of thousands of rooftop receiver boxes across an entire continent. Breaking into the trusted central management deck, a saboteur pushes one tiny remote-maintenance package down to every rooftop dish simultaneously; inside each box, the package first sweeps all ordinary storage cards and then fires raw hardware erase bolts directly into the soldered memory chips themselves, permanently silencing tens of thousands of satellite modems in one stroke. In this scenario (T1199, AcidRain MIPS ELF Satellite Modem Wiper (/dev/mtd MEMERASE / Viasat KA-SAT)), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: management Plane Compromise, then block Device Enumeration, then raw SPI Flash /dev/mtd0..99 Destruction. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering Management Plane Compromise, then Block Device Enumeration, then Raw SPI Flash /dev/mtd0..99 Destruction, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 1 with the documented host and network chain.

stages.subtitle: Initial Access & Execution (T1199 - Trusted Relationship / TR-069 Management Plane)
stages.description: Slipping past a misconfigured perimeter gate into the satellite ground-station master control room, the saboteur hijacks the official remote-update broadcaster and beams a tiny specialized demolition program simultaneously into tens of thousands of distant rooftop modems. After exploiting a VPN misconfiguration to enter the trusted management segment of the Viasat KA-SAT ground network, the threat actors issued mass management commands over the TR-069 (CWMP) protocol to deliver and execute a 140KB statically linked 32-bit MIPS ELF binary named ukrop (AcidRain) across tens of thousands of online SurfBeam2 satellite modems (Because ukrop had zero external library dependencies and brute-forced every conceivable Linux storage device path, it served as a universal embedded Linux/router/modem wiper In the documented Firewall exchange from Compromised SATCOM TR-069 ACS Server to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ACK T1199 confirming that the Stage 1: Management Plane Compromise & TR-069 CWMP Push of MIPS ELF Binary ukrop request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Stage 2: Block Device Enumeration /dev/sda, /dev/mmcblk & Sequential Overwrite). Because ukrop had zero external library dependencies and brute-forced every conceivable Linux storage device path, it served as a universal embedded Linux/router/modem wiper. In the documented Firewall exchange from Compromised SATCOM TR-069 ACS Server to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ACK T1199 (confirming that the Stage 1: Management Plane Compromise & TR-069 CWMP Push of MIPS ELF Binary (ukrop) request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Stage 2: Block Device Enumeration (/dev/sda, /dev/mmcblk) & Sequential Overwrite). stages.title: Stage 2: Block Device Enumeration (/dev/sda, /dev/mmcblk) & Sequential Overwrite
stages.subtitle: Impact (T1561.002 - Disk Structure Wipe)
stages.description: Waking up inside each modem with master system authority, the demolition program forks quietly into the background and sweeps across every attached storage partition and memory card, scrubbing every directory clean before turning to the raw hardware chips. Forking into the background as root (UID 0), AcidRain first recursively overwrote files across non-essential filesystem directories, then systematically generated device paths for /dev/sda../dev/sdz, /dev/hda../dev/hdz, /dev/mmcblk0../dev/mmcblk9, and /dev/mtdblock0../dev/mtdblock99 (overwriting the first 384KB of each device and issuing BLKDISCARD, BLKSECDISCARD, and BLKZEROOUT kernel IOCTLs to erase storage blocks). By brute-forcing hundreds of device node names in a loop, AcidRain did not need to parse /proc/partitions or sysfs and worked across any embedded Linux distribution. In the documented EDR exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to KA-SAT SurfBeam2 Modem (ukrop ELF), KA-SAT SurfBeam2 Modem (ukrop ELF) responds with ALERT T1561.002 (confirming that the Stage 2: Block Device Enumeration (/dev/sda, /dev/mmcblk) & Sequential Overwrite request succeeded on KA-SAT SurfBeam2 Modem (ukrop ELF) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Stage 3: Raw SPI Flash /dev/mtd0..99 Destruction via MEMUNLOCK, MEMERASE & MEMWRITEOOB). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ Stage 2: Block Device Enumeration (/dev/sda, /dev/mmcblk) & Sequential Overwrite / ⇠#2 ALERT T1561.002) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 KA-SAT SurfBeam2 Modem (ukrop ELF)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Bricked SPI NOR/NAND Flash & Turbines).

stages.title: Stage 3: Raw SPI Flash /dev/mtd0..99 Destruction via MEMUNLOCK, MEMERASE & MEMWRITEOOB
stages.subtitle: Impact (T1495 - Firmware Corruption / T1561.001)
stages.description: Finally, the wiper speaks straight to the modem raw soldered flash chips from slot zero through ninety-nine, reading each chip physical geometry, flipping off hardware write-locks, and issuing direct chip-erase pulses so the modem cannot even read its own startup instructions after reboot. For character-mode flash devices /dev/mtd0 through /dev/mtd99, AcidRain queried flash geometry via MEMGETINFO and then looped through every eraseblock issuing ioctl(fd, MEMUNLOCK) (unlocking software-protected flash sectors), ioctl(fd, MEMERASE) (physically erasing NOR/NAND flash blocks to 0xFF), and ioctl(fd, MEMWRITEOOB) (corrupting NAND flash Out-Of-Band ECC metadata), before invoking reboot(RB_AUTOBOOT) to permanently brick the modem. Because /dev/mtd0 holds the primary U-Boot bootloader on embedded MIPS routers and satellite modems, erasing /dev/mtd0 rendered the modems physically unbootable and required physical hardware replacement or JTAG/SPI chip reflashing. In the documented EDR exchange from KA-SAT SurfBeam2 Modem (ukrop ELF) to Linux MTD Subsystem (/dev/mtd0..99), Linux MTD Subsystem (/dev/mtd0..99) responds with ALERT T1495 (confirming that the Stage 3: Raw SPI Flash /dev/mtd0..99 Destruction via MEMUNLOCK, MEMERASE & MEMWRITEOOB request succeeded on Linux MTD Subsystem (/dev/mtd0..99) and completing the final execution objective of AcidRain MIPS ELF Satellite Modem Wiper (/dev/mtd MEMERASE / Viasat KA-SAT)). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ Stage 3: Raw SPI Flash /dev/mtd0..99 Destruction via MEMUNLOCK, MEMERASE & MEMWRITEOOB / ⇠#3 ALERT T1495) from Node ③ (#3 KA-SAT SurfBeam2 Modem (ukrop ELF)) to Node ④ (#4 Linux MTD Subsystem (/dev/mtd0..99)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Bricked SPI NOR/NAND Flash & Turbines).

keySpecs.value: ioctl(fd, MEMUNLOCK, &ei) -> ioctl(fd, MEMERASE, &ei) -> ioctl(fd, MEMWRITEOOB, &oob) -> reboot(RB_AUTOBOOT)
Hardware-lock bootloader flash sectors (`WP#` pin on SPI NOR flash) so software `MEMUNLOCK` / `MEMERASE` IOCTLs cannot erase the primary U-Boot bootloader partition (`/dev/mtd0`).
